At the end of the study, the WHO 8 Steps group reported that 74% to 94% of individuals were able to perform basic wheelchair skills, 36% to 86% could perform intermediate skills, and 2% to 29% were capable of advanced skills. In contrast, the SOC group showed that 42% to 66% of individuals could perform basic skills, and 16% to 58% could perform intermediate skills. Some skills were not achieved by any participants in these groups. The WHO 8 Steps service provision did not result in statistically significant improvements in wheelchair mobility skills, although users demonstrated the ability to perform skills ranging from basic to advanced. 2. Users reported enhanced independence, integration, and participation in daily life. Many expressed that they were now contributing to household activities rather than being perceived as a burden. Comprehensive wheelchair services based on the WHO guidelines in resource-limited settings improved mobility and functionality among participants. 3. Active occupational therapy (OT) interventions using a compiled checklist for safety, comfort, positioning, maneuverability, and transportation for wheelchair users variably impacted potential complications among adult manual wheelchair users. 4. A quasi-experimental study by Hoenig et al. found that wheelchair services provided by rehabilitation experts, including structured assessments, individually fitted wheelchairs, and additional OT/PT or home modifications, did not differ significantly from usual care in preventing worsening shoulder pain among older, physically disabled individuals. 5. A cohort study by Toro, Eke, and Pearlman in 2016 reported that at baseline, 279 participants did not have pressure sores, 23 had pressure sores, and 7 had missing data. At follow-up, 289 participants reported no pressure sores, 18 reported having them, and 2 had missing data. The WHO 8 Steps in wheelchair service provision did not significantly reduce the number of pressure sores in either group. 6. A cross-sectional study by Bazant et al. found inconsistent outcomes regarding falls among wheelchair users trained under the WHO 2008 Guidelines in Kenya and the Philippines. 7. A qualitative study by Williams et al. in 2017 described a participant with paraplegia who initially received an ill-fitting hospital-type wheelchair, leading to bedsores and a switch to crutches. This highlights complications in wheelchair services based on the WHO 2008 Guidelines. 8. A study by Beaumont-White and Ham in 1997 revealed that 67% of users received a home visit before being issued a wheelchair, 41% had a trial drive, and 74% received no therapy training. Only 63% were given a contact number for services, and 26% contacted approved repairers for repairs. The wheelchair service information sheets and booklets required improvement in content and format, and the role of referring health practitioners needed strengthening. 9. Armstrong, Reisinger, and Smith (2007) reported that the frequency of repairs for wheelchair components was generally low, except for brake handles, which required frequent repairs. The adjustable wheelchairs provided in the CIR Whirlwind project had favorable results, except for the brake handles. 10. Toro, Eke, and Pearlman (2016) found that few participants self-reported needing repairs. The WHO 8 Steps in wheelchair service provision did not result in a significant number of wheelchair repairs. 11. Beaumont-White and Ham (1997) reported that 26% of users contacted approved repairers for repairs, while 85% checked their wheelchairs themselves for faults. The referral and provision of powered wheelchair services needed review and improvement to meet user needs. 12. D’Innocenzo et al. reported that 8% of participants experienced wheelchair malfunctions or breakdowns within 3 to 6 months, with common issues including wheel lock malfunctions and bearing problems. Repairs often involved tire replacements and fixing broken wheels. 13. Gowran et al. (2020) highlighted that wheelchair users expressed concerns about inadequate repair services and the lack of a loan system for backup wheelchairs during repairs. Poor repair services were a significant issue in Irish wheelchair services. 14. A cohort study by Verza et al. examined wheelchair abandonment, while Salatino et al. highlighted that the lack of spare parts and maintenance, combined with environmental wear and tear, led to a cycle of obtaining new wheelchairs. 15. Divanoglou et al. (2019) found no changes in the total Moorong Self-Efficacy Scale (MSES) score or two of its constructs (general and social) after a 7-day active rehabilitation program for individuals with spinal cord injuries. However, the personal function construct of the MSES improved significantly. 16. Toro, Eke, and Pearlman (2016) reported that adults who received wheelchairs had significantly better environmental health scores than those on the waiting list, as measured by the WHOQOL-BREF. Female recipients also reported improved physical health, but no significant changes were observed in psychological or social relationship domains. 17. Gowran et al. (2020) emphasized the importance of wheelchairs and seating for daily performance, with participants describing them as essential for freedom, independence, quality of life, and mental health. Wheelchairs enabled users to leave their homes, work, and socialize, improving societal participation and independence. 18. Visagie et al. (2016) reported that users experienced improved independence, integration, and participation, with many feeling they were contributing to household activities rather than being a burden. 19. Hoenig et al. found that wheelchair services provided by rehabilitation experts did not differ significantly from usual care in improving wheelchair confidence among older, physically disabled individuals. 20. Salatino et al. reported that the Powered Wheelchair Effectiveness in Real Life (POWER) nine-step protocol service increased users' ability, adaptability, and self-esteem.
